profiles.title: Blanco tequila, Tequila Valley style
profiles.context: Unaged tequila from 100% blue agave, centered on the town of Tequila and the surrounding valley of Jalisco. Valley agave tends to be smaller and more herbaceous than highland agave, and many valley blancos read savory and vegetal rather than sweet.
profiles.description: A blanco (also called silver or plata) is tequila that is bottled without oak aging, so what you taste is the distilled character of the cooked agave itself: roasted piña, citrus, pepper and fresh vegetal notes. Traditional valley producers often crush the cooked agave with a tahona stone wheel and ferment in open tanks, which adds texture and a savory, earthy edge that is typical of the region. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.finish: Clean and peppery, with citrus and a gentle vegetal warmth that fades steadily.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked (oven/autoclave), tahona or roller-mill extraction, fermented in open tanks, double distilled, unaged (blanco)
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; blanco is an unaged legal class
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tequila? A blanco is the unaged version — the purest read on cooked agave, before any oak influence.

profiles.title: Espadín mezcal, Valles Centrales style
profiles.context: Artisanal joven mezcal made from espadín agave (Agave angustifolia) in the Valles Centrales around Oaxaca. Mezcal production is traditionally small-scale, with agave hearts roasted in earthen pit ovens, which gives the spirit its signature smoke. Espadín is the most widely planted mezcal agave and is often described as the most approachable of the common varieties.
profiles.description: Mezcal is a distilled spirit made from the roasted hearts of many agave species, not just blue agave. Roasting the piñas underground gives mezcal its characteristic smoke, layered over fruit, herb and mineral notes that vary with the agave variety, the village and the maestro mezcalero. This profile describes the style of a typical Valles Centrales espadín joven; individual bottles vary widely. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.smoke: Gentle to moderate smoke from the pit-roast, woven through the fruit and herb notes rather than dominating them.
profiles.finish: Long and dry, with smoke that lingers softly and fades into earthy herbs.
profiles.process: Earthen-pit roast, tahona or horse-drawn mill, wild-yeast fermentation, double distilled, joven (unaged)
profiles.category: Mezcal — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; joven/abocado is an unaged legal class
profiles.beginnerNote: New to mezcal? The smoke comes from roasting the agave underground — it is a character of the process, not an added flavor.

profiles.title: Bacanora, Agave Pacifica style (Sierra de Sonora)
profiles.context: Bacanora is a Sonoran agave spirit with a denomination of origin covering 35 municipalities in Sonora. It is distilled from Agave angustifolia pacifica (locally called Pacifica or Yaquiana), a wild-harvested agave of the Sonoran Sierra Madre. Production was banned for much of the 20th century (1915–1992) and continued clandestinely; the DO dates from 2000.
profiles.description: Traditional bacanora roasts the agave hearts in earthen pit ovens, often with mesquite wood, ferments with wild yeasts and distills twice, giving a spirit that sits stylistically between tequila and Oaxacan mezcal: roasted agave at the center with smoke that is usually gentler than mezcal's, plus desert herbs and a mineral edge from the Sierra. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Agave angustifolia pacifica (wild-harvested; locally Pacifica or Yaquiana)
profiles.process: Pit-roasted (often mesquite-fueled), wild-yeast fermentation, double distillation
profiles.category: Bacanora — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Sonora, since 2000)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to bacanora? Think of it as mezcal's Sonoran cousin: same roasted-agave heart, usually a touch less smoky, often leaner and more herbal.
profiles.smoke: Present but usually gentler than Oaxacan mezcal: the pit roast gives a lean, savory smoke rather than a dominant one.
profiles.finish: Dry and herbal, with a soft smoky thread and a mineral, peppery fade.

profiles.title: Sierra raicilla, Maximiliana style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Raicilla is a Jalisco (and one Nayarit municipality) agave spirit with a denomination of origin from 2019. It splits into two editorial traditions: Sierra (mountain) raicilla, made mainly from Agave maximiliana and inaequidens cooked in above-ground ovens, and Costa (coastal) raicilla from angustifolia and rhodacantha cooked in underground pits. This profile covers the Sierra style around the Sierra Occidental.
profiles.description: Sierra raicilla is typically cooked in above-ground adobe ovens rather than pits, so it tends to be less smoky than pit-roasted agave spirits, with a distinctive fermented, gently funky character: orchard fruit, herbs and a soft lactic roundness from wild-yeast fermentation in wooden vats. Distillation is often in small rustic stills (tabernas), and each maestro's batches vary widely. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Agave maximiliana (wild-harvested; Sierra raicilla's signature agave)
profiles.process: Above-ground adobe-oven roast, open wild-yeast fermentation in wooden vats, small-batch distillation
profiles.category: Raicilla — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Jalisco and Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, since 2019)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to raicilla? Expect an agave spirit that is often funkier and fruitier than tequila, and usually lighter on smoke than mezcal — Sierra versions especially.
profiles.smoke: Usually light in the Sierra style: above-ground ovens give a faint roast note rather than pit smoke.
profiles.finish: Medium-long, gently funky, with orchard fruit and a soft sweet-agave fade.

profiles.title: Tuxca, Liñeno/Cimarrón style (Jalisco–Colima borderlands)
profiles.context: Tuxca is a traditional agave distillate of the southern-Jalisco/northern-Colima borderlands, named for the municipality of Tuxcacuesco below the Volcán de Colima. There is no formal denomination of origin: the name is a regional tradition, not a legal category like tequila or mezcal, and definitions are loose — a working description centers production on the Río Almería valley near Tuxcacuesco, with Zapotitlán de Vadillo and Tolimán forming the historical heartland.
profiles.description: Tuxca is defined less by a legal category than by its method: wild agaves (often Liñeno/Cimarrón, i.e. Agave angustifolia and relatives) roasted in cylindrical pits, hand-mashed, fermented in volcanic stone craters, and distilled in wooden Filipino stills. The result is lean, spicy and mineral rather than smoky-sweet. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Wild agaves, often Liñeno/Cimarrón (Agave angustifolia and local relatives); ensambles vary by vinatero
profiles.process: Cylindrical pit roast, hand-mash, volcanic crater fermentation, wooden Filipino still distillation
profiles.category: Tuxca — a regional tradition with no denomination of origin; legal status is not equivalent to tequila or mezcal
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tuxca? Expect an uncertified, deeply traditional borderlands spirit — leaner and more mineral than most mezcal, with spice instead of smoke.
profiles.smoke: Usually light: the pit roast is shorter and the wooden stills read herbal-spicy rather than smoky.
profiles.finish: Dry and spicy, with lime and pepper fading to volcanic mineral.

profiles.title: Comiteco, aguamiel style (Comitán, Chiapas)
profiles.context: Comiteco comes from the municipality of Comitán de Domínguez, Chiapas, and is a sap-derived agave spirit: instead of cooking harvested agave hearts, producers collect the fresh sap (aguamiel) of the living maguey Comiteco (Agave atrovirens), ferment it, and distill it. Some comiteco includes an additional cane-based sugar source; a proposal to define the category sets a minimum of agave content rather than requiring 100% agave. Whether a specific bottle is 100% agave is a separate fact from its eligibility for this app — agave-based traditions with verified, clearly disclosed non-agave ingredients are included honestly.
profiles.description: Because the agave is never cooked, comiteco lacks the roast and smoke of pit-roasted spirits and instead shows a green, lactic, gently herbal character carried over from the fermented sap — closer in character to a distilled pulque than to mezcal, though it is its own tradition. This profile describes the style generally; compositions vary between producers and are disclosed per bottle. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Maguey Comiteco (Agave atrovirens), cultivated; sap collected from the living plant
profiles.process: Sap-derived: aguamiel collected from the living plant, fermented, distilled — no cooking of the piña
profiles.category: Comiteco — a regional tradition from Comitán, Chiapas; not a spirit with a denomination of origin, and not legally equivalent to tequila or mezcal
profiles.beginnerNote: New to comiteco? Forget smoke: this is a sap spirit — think green, lactic and herbal, from uncooked agave.
profiles.finish: Smooth and herbal, with a light earthy fade and no roast character.

profiles.title: Destilado de pulque, Salmiana style (Tlaxcala)
profiles.context: Destilado de pulque is a distilled agave-sap spirit: producers of the pulque tradition in Tlaxcala ferment the aguamiel of the maguey pulquero (Agave salmiana) into pulque, then distill it — the agave is never cooked. Tlaxcala is not part of the mezcal denomination, and destilado de pulque is not a certified category; it is a regional tradition, sold under destilado labels. Fermented pulque itself (undistilled) is not part of this spirit catalogue.
profiles.description: Distilling a fermented sap rather than a cooked agave mash gives destilado de pulque its signature: fresh, green, lactic and faintly wild, with the vegetal, slightly tangy character of pulque carried into the glass rather than roast or smoke. Reviews note everything from steamed grass and sour-candy acidity to creamed-corn sweetness — a broad, unusual range. This is editorial style guidance, not a rating of any specific bottle.
profiles.plant: Maguey pulquero (Agave salmiana); sap collected daily from the living plant
profiles.process: Sap-derived: aguamiel fermented into pulque (about 48 hours), then distilled; the piña is never cooked
profiles.category: Destilado de pulque — a regional tradition; no denomination of origin, and explicitly not mezcal (fermented pulque is not a spirit and is not catalogued here)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to destilado de pulque? It is distilled pulque — uncooked agave sap, so expect lactic, green, gently sour character unlike any cooked-agave spirit.
profiles.finish: Light and tangy, with lactic and green notes that fade quickly.
